title: Humanistic Judaism
hookLine: Sherwin Wine's Judaism of culture and ethics without theism

cards: Can a person be fully Jewish and not believe in God? You met that question on day one hundred fifty-four. Ask it around a Shabbat table and you may get a different answer from every chair.
One says no, the covenant is with God. One says of course, look at my grandfather. One says it depends on what you mean by God.

A rabbi in Michigan, Sherwin Wine, gave his answer by building something: a congregation that kept the holidays, the history, the Hebrew songs and the ethical demands of Jewish life, without addressing prayers to God.

teach.b: Humanistic Judaism. It began with one rabbi's honesty. Sherwin Wine decided he could not stand in front of a congregation and say words about God he did not believe.
Rather than leave, he looked for a way to say only what he meant. Humanistic Judaism, as his movement describes itself, is a Judaism of culture and ethics without theism. What stays?

teach.h: THE FESTIVALS STAY; THE WORDS CHANGE.
teach.b: The festivals stay: Passover, Hanukkah, the High Holy Days. Births, coming of age, weddings and funerals are marked with ceremony. The difference is in the words.
Readings speak of human courage, human history and human responsibility, rather than praying to God. Where does the weight fall? On human hands.
The Mishnah keeps a saying of Hillel: if I am not for myself, who will be for me; if I am only for myself, what am I; and if not now, when?
In a Humanistic frame, that line carries the whole load: whatever good gets done in the world, people are the ones who do it. And there is honest disagreement.

Jews in other movements push back, some strongly: for them, a Judaism without God leaves out the center, the One the Shema calls one. Humanistic Jews answer that a people, its memory and its ethics can also be a center.
Both sides are describing their own Judaism, and neither needs the other as a foil.
Some Jews say Jewish without theism, and they mean both halves of that sentence.

how: Humanistic Jewish congregations celebrate the Jewish festivals and life-cycle events with ceremonies and readings centered on human history, culture and responsibility, without prayers addressed to God.

o: a Jewish group devoted mainly to human rights campaigns
a movement that studies Jewish thinkers, not the Bible

p: a Judaism without God misses the center

games.q: you're a rabbi who can't say words about God you don't believe. what do you do?
o: build a congregation that says only what it means: culture and ethics without theism.
keep saying the words and hide your doubts.
games.why: Sherwin Wine built a congregation that kept the festivals, history and ethics and spoke of human hands rather than praying to God.

practice: Bring to mind someone who lives by strong values without belief in God, a friend, a relative, a neighbor, and one thing they do well: how they keep a promise, how they show up when someone is sick.
If you pray, you can hold them in your prayer, in your own words; if you don't, simply hold them in your attention, with respect. No arguing, no persuading, in either direction.

wordCard.voice: Humanistic Judaism. Sherwin Wine's Judaism of culture and ethics without theism: the festivals, the history and the ethics kept, with words about human hands rather than prayers to God. Today's word.
